title: The Project Partner Problem
summary: Two classmates who do not normally get along are paired for a group project and must learn to compromise and divide tasks fairly before realizing they actually work well together.
poll: Students should always be allowed to choose their own project partners instead of being assigned one.

versions.title: Working Together
versions.text:
Layla likes to plan. She makes lists. Yousef likes to work fast. He likes new things. They do not get along. They do not want to be partners.

One day, the teacher makes a new project. He puts Layla and Yousef on one team. Both groan. "Not her!" says Yousef. "Not him!" says Layla.

At first, they fight. Layla wants a plan first. Yousef wants to start right away. They do not agree.

Then they sit down. They talk. Layla says, "You can draw the chart fast. I can write the facts." Yousef smiles. "That is fair," he says.

They divide the work. Layla writes neat facts. Yousef draws fun art. The project turns out great!

The teacher feels proud. "You two did well," he says.

Layla and Yousef smile. They are glad they were partners.

versions.title: Working Together
versions.text:
Layla likes to plan and make neat lists first. Yousef likes to work fast and try new things. They do not get along well. They never want to be partners.

One day, the teacher makes a new project. He puts Layla and Yousef on the same team. Both of them groan. "Not her!" says Yousef. "Not him!" says Layla.

At first, they argue. Layla wants to make a plan first. Yousef wants to start right away. They cannot agree on it.

Then they finally sit down and talk. Layla says, "You can draw fast, since you are good at that. I can write the facts." Yousef smiles and says, "That sounds fair to me."

They divide the work. Layla writes clear, neat facts. Yousef draws fun, bright art. The project turns out great!

The teacher feels proud of their work. "You two did well," he tells them.

Layla and Yousef both smile. They are glad they were partners after all.

versions.title: The Project Partner Problem
versions.text:
Layla likes to plan things and make neat lists before she starts any task. Yousef likes to work fast and try new ideas right away, without much planning. The two of them do not get along well, and neither one wants to be partners for a class project.

One day, the teacher announces new project groups for the class. To their surprise, he puts Layla and Yousef on the same team. Both of them groan at the news. "Not her!" says Yousef under his breath. "Not him!" Layla whispers back.

At first, the two of them argue about the project. Layla wants to make a careful plan before starting. Yousef wants to jump straight into drawing. Neither one will agree with the other.

At last, they sit down and talk it through. Layla says, "You could draw fast, since that's what you're good at. I could write the facts neatly." Yousef smiles and says, "That sounds fair to me."

They divide the work fairly between them. Layla writes clear, neat facts, while Yousef draws bright, eye-catching art. Together, their project turns out looking great!

The teacher is clearly proud when he sees their finished work. "You two worked together really well," he tells them with a smile.

Layla and Yousef both grin at each other. In the end, they are glad they were paired as partners.

versions.title: The Project Partner Problem
versions.text:
Layla likes to plan things out and make neat lists before starting any task. Yousef likes to work fast and try new ideas right away. He does not spend much time on planning first. The two of them do not get along well, and neither one wants to be partners for a class project.

One day, the teacher announces new project groups for the class. To their surprise, he puts Layla and Yousef on the same team. Both of them groan at the news, clearly unhappy. "Not her!" Yousef mutters under his breath. "Not him!" Layla whispers back, just as unhappy.

At first, the two of them argue a lot about the project. Layla wants to make a careful plan before starting anything. Yousef wants to jump straight into drawing instead. Neither one will agree with the other, and both grow more upset.

After a long quiet spell, they sit down and talk it through calmly. Layla says, "You could draw fast, since that's clearly what you're good at. I could write the facts neatly instead." Yousef smiles and says, "That sounds pretty fair to me."

They divide the work fairly from that point on. Layla writes clear, neat facts about the topic, while Yousef draws bright, eye-catching art to go with them. Together, their finished project turns out looking great.

The teacher is clearly proud when he sees their work the next day. "You two worked together really well," he tells them with a warm smile.

Layla and Yousef both grin at each other, a little surprised by how well things turned out. In the end, they are glad they were paired together as partners.

versions.title: The Project Partner Problem
versions.text:
Layla liked to plan every task and build neat lists before starting. Yousef liked to work fast and test new ideas right away, rarely pausing to plan. The two of them had never gotten along well. Neither one wanted to be partners on a class project, not after their styles had clashed before.

One day, the teacher assigned new project groups. To their dismay, he placed Layla and Yousef on the same team. Both groaned at the news. "Not her," Yousef muttered, while Layla whispered back, equally frustrated, "Not him."

At first, the pair argued about the task. Layla wanted a detailed plan before touching anything else. Yousef wanted to dive straight into drawing. Neither wanted to compromise, and their frustration grew as the deadline crept closer.

At last, after a tense silence, the two sat down and talked things through. Layla offered, "You could sketch it quickly, since that's your strength. I could write out the facts." Yousef agreed at once, glad that they could finally cooperate.

From then on, they split the work by their strengths. Layla wrote clear facts, while Yousef drew bold art. Together, their project came out beautifully.

The teacher noticed this and praised their teamwork. He said they had cooperated well. Layla and Yousef traded a surprised smile, quietly beginning to appreciate a team they had not expected to enjoy.

versions.title: The Project Partner Problem
versions.text:
Layla approached nearly every task by planning carefully. She built neat lists before beginning any part of it, a habit she had rarely thought to question, let alone abandon for someone else's way of working. Yousef, by contrast, preferred working quickly and testing new ideas right away, since he found excessive planning tedious for the kind of spontaneous work he genuinely enjoyed. The two of them had never gotten along particularly well, and neither one wanted to collaborate on a class project, not after their perspectives had clashed more than once before, leaving both a little wary of working with the other again.

One morning, the teacher assigned new project groups without any warning at all. To their mutual dismay, he placed Layla and Yousef on exactly the same team, drawing a few curious glances from classmates who had clearly noticed the two did not usually get along. "Not her," Yousef muttered under his breath, while Layla whispered back, equally frustrated, "Not him."

At first, the pair argued about how to approach the task, each one certain that their own perspective was the correct one. Layla insisted on a detailed plan before touching anything else, while Yousef insisted on diving straight into drawing without delay. Neither wanted to compromise, and for a while it genuinely seemed their differences might be impossible to reconcile.

Eventually, after a tense silence between them, the two finally sat down and genuinely talked things through, each one surprising the other by actually listening for once instead of arguing over every small detail. Layla offered that Yousef could sketch quickly, since that was clearly his strength, while she could organize and write the facts carefully. Yousef agreed at once, visibly relieved that they could finally cooperate on something together.

From then on, they divided the remaining work by their own strengths, which turned out to complement each other far better than either had expected going into the project. Layla researched and wrote clear information about the topic, while Yousef illustrated it with bold artwork that caught everyone's eye right away, and together their project came together more beautifully than either of them had honestly imagined it could, finishing with time to spare before the deadline.

The teacher noticed this right away and praised their teamwork in front of the entire class, explaining to everyone that they had collaborated wonderfully despite their differences. Layla and Yousef traded a surprised smile, quietly reconciled to a team that neither of them had expected to find so invaluable, and both secretly hoped they might be paired together again on a future assignment, now that they finally understood how well their different strengths worked side by side — what had begun as an unwanted pairing had, by the end, become a lesson in how opposite approaches can sometimes produce better results than either one could have managed working entirely alone.

versions.title: The Project Partner Problem
versions.text:
Layla approached nearly every task by planning meticulously and building neat, organized lists before beginning any part of it, a habit she had relied on for as long as she could remember and had rarely thought to question, let alone abandon for someone else's unfamiliar way of working; Yousef, by contrast, preferred working quickly and testing new ideas immediately, rarely pausing to plan ahead of time, since he found excessive planning tedious and largely unnecessary for the kind of spontaneous work he genuinely enjoyed. The two of them had never gotten along particularly well, and neither one wanted to collaborate on a class project, not after their very different perspectives had clashed more than once before, leaving both of them a little wary of working with the other again.

One day, the teacher assigned new project groups to the entire class without any warning at all, and to their mutual dismay, he placed Layla and Yousef on exactly the same team, drawing a few curious glances from classmates who had clearly noticed the two did not usually get along; "Not her," Yousef muttered under his breath, while Layla whispered back, just as unhappily, "Not him."

At first, the pair argued endlessly about how to approach the assignment, each one certain that their own perspective was the correct one: Layla insisted on building a detailed plan before touching anything else, while Yousef insisted on diving straight into drawing without delay, and neither wanted to compromise, so that for a while it seemed their differences might be impossible to reconcile, no matter how much time they were given to work things out.

Eventually, after a tense silence between them, the two finally sat down and genuinely talked things through, each one surprising the other by actually listening for once instead of arguing over every small detail; Layla offered that Yousef could sketch the poster quickly, since that was clearly his strength, while she could organize and write the facts carefully, and Yousef agreed instantly, visibly relieved that they could finally cooperate on something together rather than fighting over it.

From then on, they divided the remaining work according to their individual strengths, which turned out to complement each other far better than either had expected going into the project: Layla researched and wrote clear, organized information about the topic, while Yousef illustrated it with bold, colorful artwork that caught everyone's eye immediately, and together their project came together more beautifully than either of them had honestly imagined it could, finishing with time to spare before the deadline.

The teacher noticed immediately and praised their teamwork in front of the entire class, telling them that they had collaborated wonderfully; Layla and Yousef exchanged a surprised smile, quietly reconciled to a partnership that neither of them had expected to find so invaluable, and both secretly hoped they might be paired together again on a future assignment.

Looking back, what had begun as an unwanted pairing became, by the end, a lesson in how opposite approaches can sometimes produce far better results than either person could have managed working alone: Layla learned that moving quickly did not always mean working carelessly, while Yousef learned that careful planning could sharpen, rather than slow down, a good idea, and neither of them abandoned their own natural way of working, discovering instead how to let two very different strengths support one another rather than compete.

keyWords.definition: a person you work together with on a task
keyWords.example: My partner and I built a model volcano for class.

keyWords.definition: a piece of work, often done over several days, usually about one topic
keyWords.example: Our class project this month is about the ocean.

keyWords.definition: to split something into parts and share it
keyWords.example: We divided the chores so everyone had a job.

keyWords.definition: treating everyone in a way that is right and equal
keyWords.example: The teacher gave everyone a fair turn to speak.

keyWords.definition: to have the same opinion as someone else
keyWords.example: The two friends finally agreed on a movie to watch.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Two students studying for a difficult science test in the library
Two classmates who don't get along learning to work together
A boy who loses his favorite pet at school and looks for it
A class building a small house out of wood in the yard
questions.why: The story follows Layla and Yousef, who do not get along at first but learn to work together well on a class project.

wrong.A: The story is about a project, not studying for a test.
wrong.C: The story does not mention a lost pet.
wrong.D: The class does not build a house in the story.

questions.stem: What does the teacher do that surprises Layla and Yousef?
options: He puts the two of them in the same project group
He cancels the class project for everyone
He gives the whole class a surprise test instead
He sends Layla and Yousef home early that day
questions.why: The teacher makes new project groups and places Layla and Yousef on the same team, which upsets them both.

wrong.B: The project still happens; it is not canceled.
wrong.C: The story does not mention a surprise test.
wrong.D: Neither student is sent home in the story.

questions.stem: How do Layla and Yousef divide the work on their project?
options: They both only draw pictures and nothing else all day
They both write facts and skip the pictures
Yousef writes the facts, and Layla draws
Layla writes the facts, and Yousef draws the pictures
questions.why: Layla agrees to write the facts neatly, while Yousef draws the colorful pictures for the poster.

wrong.A: Layla writes the facts; she does not draw.
wrong.B: Yousef draws the pictures; he does not write the facts.
wrong.C: They finish the project together and it turns out great.

questions.stem: Why do Layla and Yousef argue at first about the project?
options: They disagree about which topic their project should cover
They argue over who gets to keep a pencil
They want to do the project in very different ways
They argue about what to eat for lunch that day
questions.why: Layla wants to plan carefully first, while Yousef wants to start drawing right away, so they cannot agree.

wrong.A: The story does not say they disagree about the topic.
wrong.B: The story does not mention a pencil.
wrong.D: The story does not mention lunch.

questions.stem: Why does Yousef agree that dividing the work this way is fair?
options: Because each of them gets to do the part they are good at
Because Layla forces him to agree with her plan
Because he wants to finish quickly and go home
Because the teacher orders him to agree with Layla and work with her
questions.why: Yousef gets to draw, which he enjoys and is good at, while Layla writes the facts, which she enjoys and is good at.

wrong.B: The two of them talk calmly and decide together; Layla does not force him.
wrong.C: The story does not say Yousef just wants to leave quickly.
wrong.D: The teacher does not order them; the plan comes from Layla and Yousef themselves.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Layla and Yousef by the end of the story?
options: They still do not like each other in the end
They decide they will never work together again
They work well together even though they are different
They become exactly the same in how they like to work
questions.why: By the end, Layla and Yousef are smiling and glad they were partners, even though their styles are different.

wrong.A: They end up smiling and happy with each other.
wrong.B: They are glad to have worked together, not against it.
wrong.D: They keep their own different styles; they do not become the same.

questions.stem: In the story, the word partners means —
options: people who work together on something
people who never speak to each other
people who compete against each other
people who live in the same house
questions.why: Layla and Yousef become partners, meaning they work together on the project.

wrong.B: Partners usually talk and work together, not avoid speaking.
wrong.C: Partners work on the same side, not against each other.
wrong.D: The story does not say they live together.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe Layla and Yousef as having different styles at the beginning?
options: To help readers see why their later teamwork is surprising
To explain the steps for making a neat list
To compare Layla and Yousef's two different schools and their teachers
To describe all of the teacher's classroom rules
questions.why: Showing how different they are at the start makes their later success working together feel more surprising and important.

wrong.B: The story does not teach how to make a list.
wrong.C: Layla and Yousef attend the same school and class.
wrong.D: The story does not describe a full list of classroom rules.

LOW.prompt: Do you think Layla and Yousef made a good decision about how to divide their work? Explain why or why not, using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think Layla and Yousef made a good decision. Layla wrote the facts neatly because she is good at planning, and Yousef drew the fun pictures because he is good at working fast. Their project looked great because they each did the part they were best at.

keyWords.definition: to give up part of what you want so that each side can agree
keyWords.example: The brothers compromised by sharing the video game, thirty minutes each.

keyWords.definition: to work together with someone to get something done
keyWords.example: The whole team cooperated to clean up the park in one afternoon.

keyWords.definition: to give someone a particular task or group to be part of
keyWords.example: The coach assigned each player to a position on the field.

keyWords.definition: feeling annoyed or upset because something is difficult or not going well
keyWords.example: She felt frustrated when her computer kept freezing during homework.

keyWords.definition: to recognize the value of something and feel grateful for it
keyWords.example: He finally appreciated how much work his sister had put into the gift.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: The teacher decides that class projects are no longer necessary for anyone in the whole school this year
Two classmates with opposite working styles learn to compromise and discover they make a strong team
Yousef realizes that drawing pictures is more important than writing facts for a report
Layla and Yousef are best friends from the very first day of school, and they never argue
questions.why: The story shows Layla and Yousef overcoming their initial conflict by compromising, and discovering they actually work well as a team.

wrong.A: The teacher still assigns the project; he does not remove it.
wrong.C: Both writing and drawing matter equally to the finished project.
wrong.D: Layla and Yousef do not get along at the start of the story.

questions.stem: What does Layla insist on doing before starting the project?
options: Building a detailed plan before doing anything else
Asking the teacher to choose a different topic for them
Drawing the poster herself before Yousef can touch it
Finishing the entire project on her own
questions.why: Layla insists on building a detailed plan before starting any other part of the project.

wrong.B: The story does not say Layla asks for a different topic.
wrong.C: Layla focuses on writing the facts, not on drawing.
wrong.D: Layla and Yousef ultimately work together, not alone.

questions.stem: According to the story, what does Yousef do with the poster?
options: He refuses to work on the poster
He writes most of the factual information for it
He illustrates it with bold, colorful artwork
He throws the poster away before it is finished
questions.why: Yousef illustrates the poster with bold, colorful artwork while Layla handles the research and writing.

wrong.A: Yousef works eagerly on the poster's artwork.
wrong.B: Layla writes the factual information, not Yousef.
wrong.D: The finished poster turns out beautifully and is not thrown away.

questions.stem: What happens right after Layla and Yousef argue endlessly about the assignment?
options: The teacher separates them into two different groups, and each one works alone
After a tense silence, the two finally sit down and talk things through
Yousef quits the project and refuses to continue, so Layla must do all of it
Layla finishes the whole project by herself that same day, and Yousef just watches
questions.why: After their argument, a tense silence passes, and then the two finally sit down together and talk things through calmly.

wrong.A: The teacher does not separate them into different groups.
wrong.C: Yousef continues working on the project; he does not quit.
wrong.D: Layla does not finish the project alone; they work together.

questions.stem: Why does Yousef's frustration grow before the two classmates finally talk?
options: Because Layla refuses to speak to him during that time, and walks away
Because the deadline is getting closer while neither is willing to compromise
Because the teacher keeps changing the project's topic every week
Because Yousef realizes he dislikes drawing pictures for the class
questions.why: As the deadline approaches and neither Layla nor Yousef will compromise, their disagreement remains unresolved and frustration builds.

wrong.A: Layla and Yousef do speak, even though they argue.
wrong.C: The story does not say the teacher changes the topic.
wrong.D: Yousef enjoys drawing; it becomes his part of the project.

questions.stem: What does the teacher's praise suggest about how Layla and Yousef's different approaches worked together?
options: Their different strengths combined to produce better results than either could alone
Only Layla's careful planning truly mattered to the finished project, and Yousef's drawing was never used
Yousef's quick drawing mattered most to the finished project, and Layla's planning was hardly used
Their different approaches canceled each other out, so the teacher was unhappy
questions.why: The teacher's praise for their teamwork shows that combining Layla's organization with Yousef's artwork produced a strong result.

wrong.B: Yousef's artwork is also an important part of the finished project.
wrong.C: Layla's organized facts are also an important part of the finished project.
wrong.D: The project turns out beautifully, not as nothing achieved.

questions.stem: In the story, the word compromise means —
options: to win every single part of an argument completely
to give up part of what you want so each side can agree
to refuse to speak with someone ever again
to copy exactly what another person wants to do
questions.why: Layla and Yousef compromise by each giving up part of their original plan so they can agree on a fair way to divide the work.

wrong.A: Compromise means neither side wins everything; both sides adjust.
wrong.C: Compromise requires communication, not silence.
wrong.D: Compromise is a shared agreement, not simply copying one side.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the story?
options: By listing numbered steps for creating a neat poster
By comparing Layla and Yousef's project with another group's project in the same class
By describing their differences, then the conflict, then how they resolve it
By describing one entire school year, from the first day to the last
questions.why: The story first introduces their contrasting styles, then the conflict over the project, and finally how they compromise and succeed together.

wrong.A: The story is not a list of steps for making a poster.
wrong.B: The story does not compare their project with another group's.
wrong.D: The story focuses on one project, not an entire school year.

MID.prompt: Explain how Layla and Yousef's different working styles ended up helping, rather than hurting, their project. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how their different styles helped the project.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: At first, Layla and Yousef's different styles caused arguments, since Layla wanted to plan carefully while Yousef wanted to start drawing right away. Once they compromised, though, their differences actually helped the project: Layla researched and wrote clear, organized facts, while Yousef illustrated the poster with bold, colorful artwork. Together, these two different strengths combined to make a project that the teacher praised in front of the whole class.

keyWords.definition: to work together with someone else to produce or achieve something
keyWords.example: The two scientists collaborated on a study about desert plants.

keyWords.definition: a particular way of viewing or thinking about a situation
keyWords.example: Hearing her grandmother's perspective helped her understand the old photograph.

keyWords.definition: to go well with something else and make it better as a result
keyWords.example: The spicy sauce complemented the mild rice perfectly.

keyWords.definition: to settle a disagreement or bring differing ideas into agreement
keyWords.example: The committee worked for weeks to reconcile the two competing proposals.
Her uncle's advice about saving money proved invaluable later in life.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the passage?
options: The teacher's assigned groups turn out to be a disaster for everyone involved, so students should pick their own partners
Two students with conflicting approaches to work discover that their differences, once reconciled, can complement rather than undermine each other
Careful planning is a better approach to any project than quick, spontaneous action, and students should never change a plan once it is made
Yousef gives up his own working style to satisfy Layla, and he stops working that way
questions.why: The passage shows that Layla's careful planning and Yousef's quick action, once reconciled, complement one another and improve the project.

wrong.A: This particular assigned pairing turns out well, not disastrously.
wrong.C: The passage shows both approaches have value once combined, not that one is simply better.
wrong.D: Neither of them gives up their own way of working.

questions.stem: What realization does Layla come to, according to the passage's final paragraph?
options: That moving quickly does not always mean working carelessly
That Yousef's drawings were never actually useful to the project
That planning is completely unnecessary for any class project
That the teacher's assigned groups should be abolished entirely
questions.why: At the end, Layla learns that working fast does not always mean working carelessly.

wrong.B: Yousef's artwork is a valuable, appreciated part of the finished project.
wrong.C: Layla continues valuing planning; she simply reconsiders quickness too.
wrong.D: The passage does not suggest ending assigned groups generally.

questions.stem: What realization does Yousef come to, according to the passage's final paragraph?
options: That Layla's facts were ultimately unnecessary for the poster in the end
That drawing quickly is inferior to drawing slowly and with care
That careful planning could sharpen, rather than slow down, a good idea
That he should never attempt another class project again, even with a friend
questions.why: At the end, Yousef learns that careful planning can make a good idea better instead of slowing it down.

wrong.A: Layla's facts are a valued, necessary part of the finished poster.
wrong.B: The passage contrasts fast and careful work without ranking one as always worse.
wrong.D: Yousef hopes to be paired with Layla again on a future project.

questions.stem: What does the pair's initial certainty that their 'own perspective was the correct one' suggest about why they struggled to cooperate at first?
options: Each assumed there was only one right way to work, leaving no room for compromise
Neither of them actually cared at all about the project's outcome
They had never met each other before being placed in the same group
The teacher had secretly instructed them not to cooperate with each other on the project
questions.why: Believing their own approach was the only correct one left little space for either student to compromise, which fueled the early conflict.

wrong.B: Both care enough about the project to argue passionately over how to do it.
wrong.C: The passage implies they already knew each other and had clashed before.
wrong.D: The teacher praises their eventual teamwork, showing he wanted them to cooperate.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest by noting that neither of them gave up their own way of working?
options: Their final project failed because neither one of them would adapt or change at all, and they argued all week long
Layla eventually started working exactly the way Yousef always had, and she gave up her own way
Yousef eventually started working exactly the way Layla always had, and he gave up his own way
Successful collaboration did not require either person to change who they were, only how they worked together
questions.why: The passage shows both students kept their own strengths while learning to combine them productively, rather than one replacing the other.

wrong.A: Their project succeeds and earns praise, rather than failing.
wrong.B: Layla keeps her careful, organized approach throughout the passage.
wrong.C: Yousef keeps his quick, creative approach throughout the passage.

questions.stem: In the passage, the word invaluable most nearly means —
options: extremely valuable or important
having no value or worth
difficult to measure in size or weight
likely to disappear very soon
questions.why: The partnership turns out to be invaluable, meaning extremely valuable, to both Layla and Yousef.

wrong.B: Invaluable means extremely valuable, nearly the opposite of worthless.
wrong.C: Invaluable describes worth, not physical size or weight.
wrong.D: Invaluable describes lasting worth, not something about to vanish.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the passage by explaining what each character personally learned?
options: To argue that the teacher deserves all of the credit for their success in the whole project
To suggest that Layla learned the most from the experience
To show that the resolution changed both characters' understanding, not just their project's outcome
To prove that group projects should be assigned randomly in classes from now on
questions.why: Describing what both Layla and Yousef individually learned emphasizes that their growth, not only their finished poster, was an important result of the story.

wrong.A: The credit in the passage goes mainly to the students' own compromise.
wrong.B: The passage describes lessons learned by both Yousef and Layla.
wrong.D: The passage does not make a general argument about how groups should always be assigned.

questions.stem: How does Layla's approach to the project compare with Yousef's throughout the passage?
options: Layla cared only about drawing, while Yousef cared only about writing facts, and they never worked together on the poster
Layla and Yousef approached the project in the same careful, planned way, so they rarely argued
Layla and Yousef approached the project in the same quick way, so they made no plan for it
Layla favored careful planning, while Yousef favored quick action, and both approaches proved valuable once combined
questions.why: Layla's careful planning and Yousef's quick, creative action were different, but the passage shows both ultimately strengthened the finished project.

wrong.A: Layla focuses on the facts, while Yousef focuses on the drawing, the reverse of this option.
wrong.B: Yousef prefers quick action rather than careful planning.
wrong.C: Layla prefers careful planning rather than quick action.

HIGH.prompt: The poll suggests students should always choose their own project partners rather than being assigned one. Using evidence from the passage, argue for or against this idea.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the passage.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that students should always choose their own partners, because the passage shows how much Layla and Yousef gained from an assigned pairing they did not want. Despite their clashing perspectives, they were forced to reconcile their differences, and Layla's organized research ended up complementing Yousef's bold artwork far better than either expected. Someone might argue that students work best with friends who already get along, but the passage suggests the opposite: Layla and Yousef's collaboration became invaluable precisely because their differing strengths, not their similarity, made the finished project stronger than either could have produced alone.

LOW.stem: What does Layla like to make?
options: Fast drawings
New toys
Lists
Funny jokes
LOW.why: The text says Layla likes to plan and makes lists.

wrong.A: Yousef is the one who draws the art.
wrong.B: The text does not say she makes toys.
wrong.D: The text does not say she makes jokes.

LOW.stem: In the story, what does "groan" mean?
options: To make a sad sound when unhappy
To jump up and cheer with joy
To whisper a secret to a friend
To clap your hands for a team
LOW.why: Both students groan when they hear they are partners, because they do not want to work together.

wrong.B: They are not cheering; they say "Not her" and "Not him."
wrong.C: They talk out loud, not in secret.
wrong.D: They are not happy about the team.

LOW.stem: What happens right after Layla and Yousef fight about the plan?
options: They go home early
They ask a new partner to join
The teacher ends the project
They sit down and talk
LOW.why: In the story, after they argue, they sit down and talk.

wrong.A: They stay and work on the project.
wrong.B: No new partner joins them.
wrong.C: The project goes on and turns out great.

LOW.stem: Why does the teacher feel proud?
options: The two worked well and made a great project
The class got the day off from school
Yousef finished the work before Layla
Layla and Yousef changed their teacher's mind
LOW.why: In the story, they work together and the project turns out great, so the teacher is proud.

wrong.B: The text does not say anything about a day off.
wrong.C: The work was shared, and there was no race.
wrong.D: The teacher did not change his mind; he is just proud.

MID.stem: What did Yousef like to do when he started a task?
options: Make a neat list before anything else
Ask the teacher for a full plan
Work fast and test new ideas right away
Wait and watch what his partner did
MID.why: In the text, Yousef liked to work fast and test new ideas right away.

wrong.A: Making neat lists is what Layla does.
wrong.B: Nothing says he asked for a plan; he rarely planned.
wrong.D: He wanted to start, not wait.

MID.stem: In the story, the word "dismay" means —
options: great joy and pride
a feeling of being tired
a happy surprise
a feeling of being upset
MID.why: They groaned and muttered when they were placed on the same team, so dismay means they felt upset.

wrong.A: They were not joyful at the news.
wrong.B: Tiredness is not the reason they groaned.
wrong.C: They did not like the surprise.

MID.stem: Why did Layla and Yousef groan at the news from the teacher?
options: They did not get along and did not want to be partners
They thought the project would be far too easy for them
They had already finished all of the project
They wanted to work alone on a big poster
MID.why: The two had never gotten along well and neither wanted to be partners.

wrong.B: They were upset about the partner, not about the work being easy.
wrong.C: The project was just being assigned.
wrong.D: The text does not mention a poster.

MID.stem: What does the ending suggest about how Layla and Yousef feel about working together?
options: They want to work alone next time
They are still angry at each other
They now like the team more than they expected
They wish the teacher chose new partners
MID.why: They share a surprised smile and begin to appreciate a team they had not expected to enjoy.

wrong.A: They are starting to appreciate the team.
wrong.B: They exchange a smile, so they are not angry.
wrong.D: They are beginning to enjoy the team they got.

HIGH.stem: How did the teacher announce the new project groups?
options: With a long speech about teamwork
After each student chose a friend
With a vote by the whole class
Without any warning
HIGH.why: The text says the teacher assigned new project groups without any warning.

wrong.A: No speech about teamwork is mentioned.
wrong.B: The teacher chose the groups; students did not.
wrong.C: No class vote is mentioned.

HIGH.stem: In the passage, what does the phrase "impossible to reconcile" mean?
options: Too funny to talk about at all
Too small to matter very much
Impossible to bring into agreement
Too old to be remembered well
HIGH.why: The pair kept arguing, so their differences seemed impossible to bring into agreement.

wrong.A: Their argument was not funny.
wrong.B: Their differences felt big to them.
wrong.D: The argument was happening now.

HIGH.stem: What helped Layla and Yousef stop arguing?
options: The teacher chose a new partner for each
They sat down and talked things through
Their classmates told them what to do
They agreed to follow Layla's plan only
HIGH.why: After a tense silence, the two sat down and genuinely talked things through.

wrong.A: The teacher did not change the partners.
wrong.C: The classmates only glanced at them.
wrong.D: They agreed to divide the work by strengths, not to follow only Layla's plan.

HIGH.stem: Why does the author include the whispered lines "Not her" and "Not him"?
options: To show both felt the same frustration
To show that the classmates were laughing
To show that the teacher was angry
To show the project was already done
HIGH.why: Yousef and Layla say nearly the same thing, which shows they both felt upset about the pairing.

wrong.B: The classmates only gave curious glances.
wrong.C: The teacher is not shown as angry.
wrong.D: The project has not started yet at that point.
